title: NASA Chandra Finds the Hidden Stellar Corpse Behind a 14-Year Supernova Impostor Mystery
excerpt: Supernova impostor AT 2016blu erupted 27 times in 14 years without dying. NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory now confirms a hidden compact object -- a black hole or neutron star -- was orbiting alongside it and triggering each outburst. Published November 9 in The Astrophysical Journal, the study
content:
For 14 years, astronomers watched a massive star in a nearby galaxy throw what looked like a tantrum — erupting in a blaze of light 27 separate times, mimicking a supernova again and again, without ever destroying itself. Now, thanks to a precisely timed observation by NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory, they finally know why: a hidden stellar corpse orbiting alongside it was pulling matter off the star at every close approach, triggering each outburst like clockwork.

The discovery, published in The Astrophysical Journal on November 9, 2026, identifies AT 2016blu as the first known "supernova impostor" star confirmed to have a compact object — a black hole or neutron star — as a companion. It transforms a stubborn astrophysical mystery into a window on some of the most extreme physics in the universe.

"Until we were able to get Chandra data at the right time, we couldn't figure out what was making this happen," said lead author Mojgan Aghakhanloo of the University of Virginia. "It's like having a front row seat to seeing what the star is doing before it dies."

A Star That Kept Faking Its Own Death

AT 2016blu sits in NGC 4559, a spiral galaxy about 30 million light-years from Earth. It belongs to a rare class of cosmic giants called luminous blue variables (LBVs) — stars so massive and unstable that they periodically shed enormous amounts of material in eruptions far more energetic than ordinary stellar winds. When an LBV erupts brightly enough to resemble a supernova from Earth without actually destroying itself, astronomers call it a "supernova impostor."

What made AT 2016blu unusual even among impostors was its relentless regularity. Beginning in 2012, surveys caught it erupting again and again on a cycle of roughly 113 days — 27 outbursts confirmed through mid-2026, watched by ground-based telescopes, robotic survey cameras, and thousands of amateur astronomers coordinating through the American Association of Variable Star Observers (AAVSO).

"Clearly it's not [dying]," said co-author Núria Torres-Albà of the University of Virginia, "because it keeps surviving these outbursts about three times a year."

That clockwork regularity was the key clue. Random stellar instability doesn't repeat on a precise schedule. Something gravitational was clearly involved — an orbital period.

What Chandra Found: X-Rays That Betrayed a Hidden Companion

The team suspected a compact companion was driving the outbursts, but proving it required catching the star during an eruption in X-rays. Chandra's Target of Opportunity program lets astronomers interrupt scheduled observations for time-critical events, and in March 2026, that program paid off: the team triggered a Chandra observation timed precisely to AT 2016blu's predicted outburst peak.

What they found was unambiguous. During the outburst, the star's X-ray brightness jumped to more than 100 times its pre-outburst level, reaching an X-ray luminosity of log L_X ≈ 38.64 ± 0.11 erg per second — equivalent to roughly 100 trillion times the total energy output of the Sun, expressed in X-rays alone. That X-ray signal is the fingerprint of accretion: matter falling at high speed onto a dense, compact object and heating to temperatures of tens of millions of degrees as it falls.

The implied accretion rate — the amount of stellar material falling onto the companion — came to at least 8 × 10⁻⁸ solar masses per year, entirely consistent with a neutron star or stellar-mass black hole feeding from the wind of a massive companion star.

How the Mechanism Works

The physics is as elegant as it is violent. AT 2016blu and its compact companion orbit each other on an elliptical path, like a highly stretched-out oval. Every 113 days, the two objects sweep to their closest approach — called periastron — and the compact object's gravitational field sweeps up a surge of material from the LBV's powerful stellar wind.

That infalling matter doesn't simply land on the compact object. It forms a rotating disk of increasingly hot gas spiraling inward. As the material compresses and accelerates, it radiates — first as visible light, then as ultraviolet radiation, and finally, at temperatures approaching 10 million degrees Celsius (18 million degrees Fahrenheit), as X-rays. The result is a brief, brilliant flare visible across millions of light-years.

After periastron, the two stars move apart along their elongated orbit. The accretion rate drops, the X-ray emission fades, and the system returns to relative quiet until the orbit brings them close again. The 27 outbursts documented between 2012 and 2026 are, in effect, 27 periastron passages.

"So, we needed to plan the Chandra X-ray observations carefully to be simultaneous with an optical outburst," said co-author Nathan Smith of the University of Arizona.

Why This Discovery Required Chandra — And Only Chandra

The confirmation of AT 2016blu's compact companion wasn't just a matter of pointing a telescope at the right star at the right time. It required a capability that exists in exactly one X-ray telescope currently in operation.

About 10 arcseconds away from AT 2016blu on the sky — an angular separation roughly equivalent to a quarter-inch at 100 feet — sits another X-ray source called NGC 4559 X7, a known ultraluminous X-ray source (ULX) that is actually far more luminous than AT 2016blu in outburst. At the resolution of any other X-ray telescope, the two sources would have blurred into one, making it impossible to attribute the X-ray emission to AT 2016blu specifically.

Chandra's mirror system produces the sharpest X-ray images ever achieved, capable of separating sources that are fractions of an arcsecond apart. That angular precision — built into the observatory's 24-year-old mirror assembly — is not currently matched by any other instrument in space. Without it, the compact companion would have remained hidden inside a smear of combined X-ray light from two different sources.

This matters beyond the specific discovery: Chandra is currently navigating a funding crisis, with proposed NASA budget cuts that have threatened to sharply curtail or end the observatory's operations within the next few years. AT 2016blu is a concrete demonstration of science that is simply not possible without it.

A Black Hole or Neutron Star — And We Don't Yet Know Which

The study confirms that AT 2016blu's companion is a compact object — the collapsed remnant of a star that ended its life in a supernova — but cannot yet determine whether that remnant is a neutron star or a black hole.

Distinguishing the two typically requires detecting X-ray pulsations (a neutron star spinning rapidly can produce a lighthouse-like pulse detectable from Earth), observing a thermonuclear flash on a neutron star's hard surface, or measuring the companion's mass through precise spectroscopic observations. None of these has been possible for AT 2016blu yet.

What the team can say is that the X-ray luminosity and inferred accretion rate are consistent with both possibilities. Interestingly, the nearby ULX NGC 4559 X7 — the source that complicated the X-ray analysis — has itself shown evidence in a 2025 Pintore et al. study for pulsations suggesting a neutron star. The same region of NGC 4559 may host two separate compact-object binaries of different kinds.

"We know a lot about them, but also there are a lot of open questions," Aghakhanloo said. "We still don't fully understand how they evolve or how they die."

A Progenitor of Gravitational Waves?

The implications of the AT 2016blu system extend beyond stellar astrophysics. When AT 2016blu eventually exhausts its nuclear fuel and explodes in a true supernova — an event that could happen in the astronomically near future, within the next tens of thousands of years — it will leave behind a second compact object: another neutron star or black hole.

What remains will be a double compact object binary: two stellar remnants in a tight mutual orbit. Over millions of years, gravitational wave emission will shrink their orbit until the two remnants spiral into each other and merge. That merger is precisely the kind of event detected by the LIGO-Virgo gravitational-wave network since 2015 — and one of the outstanding questions in astrophysics is how systems like these form in sufficient numbers to explain the detection rate.

AT 2016blu offers a rare observational glimpse of a system that may be on this exact evolutionary pathway. The LBV phase is so brief — lasting only tens of thousands of years compared to a stellar lifetime of millions — that catching a compact object in orbit around an LBV star is an opportunity that may not come twice.

What Comes Next

The team has already secured additional Chandra time to study AT 2016blu and to search for other LBV systems that may harbor hidden compact companions. The discovery was enabled in part by the decade-long photometric record built by amateur astronomers, whose systematic monitoring established the 113-day orbital period in the first place.

Future surveys, particularly the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time scheduled to begin full operations in 2026, will scan the southern sky repeatedly over ten years — generating the kind of multi-year variability record that makes discoveries like this one possible at a far larger scale. If other LBV+compact-object binaries exist in nearby galaxies, Rubin's survey should surface them.

For now, AT 2016blu stands as the first confirmed member of a class of binary systems that may ultimately tell us how some of the universe's most extreme mergers — and their gravitational-wave aftershocks — are born.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Is a Supernova Impostor?

A supernova impostor is a massive star that undergoes a catastrophic eruption powerful enough to resemble a supernova from Earth, but survives the event. Unlike a true supernova — which destroys the star — an impostor is driven by the star temporarily exceeding its own luminosity limit, ejecting material in a giant flare. The most famous example in our galaxy is the Eta Carinae system, which erupted in the 1840s and briefly became the second-brightest star in the sky.

What Is a Luminous Blue Variable?

Luminous blue variables are among the most massive and unstable stars known — typically 20 to more than 100 times the mass of the Sun. They occupy an unstable region of the stellar temperature-luminosity diagram, where their enormous radiation pressure competes with gravity for control of the outer layers. The result is semi-regular eruptions, variable brightness, and rapid, dramatic changes in stellar structure. The term was coined by astronomer Peter Conti in 1984; fewer than 20 confirmed LBVs are known in the Milky Way, with AT 2016blu being an example in a nearby galaxy.

What Does Accretion Have to Do With X-Rays?

When matter falls onto a compact object — a neutron star or black hole — it converts gravitational potential energy into kinetic energy and then heat with extraordinary efficiency. The infalling gas can reach temperatures of 10 million to 100 million degrees Celsius (18 million to 180 million degrees Fahrenheit), far hotter than any ordinary stellar process. At those temperatures, the gas radiates primarily in the X-ray band of the electromagnetic spectrum, which is why X-ray telescopes like Chandra are uniquely suited to studying accretion-powered systems.
